svg.title: Fifteen minutes into the first unit of packed red cells, a 55-year-old woman develops chills and low back pain. Her temperature has risen from 36.8 °C to 38.6 °C and her blood pressure has fallen from 124/70 to 96/54. The urine in her catheter bag is dark red-brown.
svg.desc: Fever, flank or back pain, and hemoglobinuria within the first hour of a transfusion suggest an acute hemolytic reaction, and the first step is always to stop the transfusion. Normal saline through separate tubing keeps the vein available without pushing any more incompatible cells in. Slowing the rate is tempting because it feels less drastic, but even a small extra volume adds to the hemolysis. The unit and tubing are saved and returned for investigation, not discarded.
